quote: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
As we sleep, and during quiet rest, the hippocampus replays our recent experiences.
Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context.
The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).
Claude can use dreaming to organize memory. This can correct mistakes, create notes, build new memory representations, or shape what’s preemptively loaded into future sessions.

By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later.

It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction
But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again.
After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next.
Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed.
Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.

Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.

Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.
Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date.

Its global.md file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory.

Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.
We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it.
When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right).
For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.
prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left).
Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.

With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up.

At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.”
Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.
Claude checked the note against the session transcript, caught its error, and rewrote it. The transcript gave Claude a ground truth to validate its memory against.
With the corrected memory note, Claude went straight back into Mt. Moon and eventually reached Cerulean City.

In the run with the uncorrected note, Claude dropped back onto that earlier route three times. After the third failure, Claude seemed to give up, writing, “I’m going to stop rather than keep looping.”
The run ended without Claude ever reaching Cerulean City.
One type of memory representation it uses is called a wiki, a collection of pages written and maintained by Claude that gathers what Claude knows about one subject and links it to other notes.

about 350,000 files, roughly 420M tokens—from Stainless, a software company we acquired in May. We created an evaluation set of 25 questions about this corpus and gave Claude a search tool to explore it.
Over 128 sessions, we prompted Opus 5 agents to explore the files, write or correct linked wiki pages, merge duplicates, and check claims against the sources.
As we scaled dreaming from two sessions to 128, performance on the 25 questions grew from 13% to 48% of graded criteria (Figure 10).
When it used both search and the wiki, Claude’s aggregate score rose from 54% to 61% as that wiki grew, compared with 53% when it had access to the search tool alone.
Using search and the wiki also saved about 20,000 tokens per question.

But logging notes in the moment inevitably draws Claude’s attention away from its main task. In contrast, dreaming can push memory creation to the background, but any outputs from dreaming may not be immediately accessible to Claude.
Dreaming is one way to fix these mistakes (Figure 8), but it requires compute. Directing Claude to continuously check all its memories might not be practical.
It may be important instead to focus dreaming on information that’s likely to change or to carefully tune the cadence of dreaming (e.g., based on how often memories are accessed).
It’s also reasonable to consider transcript search as the foundation of Claude’s memory.
But Claude needs to use compute to maintain memory representations and make sure they don’t accumulate errors or hallucinations.
Even though Claude’s judgment about salience has improved, no model can really know what will happen in future turns.

Dreaming is a scheduled process in Claude Managed Agents that reviews agent sessions and memory stores, extracts patterns, and curates memories so agents improve over time. You decide how much control you want: dreaming can update memory automatically, or you can review changes before they land.
Dreaming is available in Managed Agents on the Claude Platform; developers can request access here.
Dreaming is available in research preview, outcomes, multiagent orchestration, and memory are available in public beta as part of Managed Agents.

The first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md`, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation. Content beyond that threshold is not loaded at session start. Claude keeps `MEMORY.md` concise by moving detailed notes into separate topic files.
